$comment: schema mentor.build/v1 — the third instance, and the one that closes the
pricing/ is `authored` (a history written up afterwards). safety-gear/ is
`observed` (the checkpoint tracker recorded it as the work happened). This one
is `git` — derived from real commits, where nobody's memory is involved at all.
Three fixtures, three provenance levels, and MENTOR's confidence rises across
them because the evidence genuinely improves rather than because a number was
tuned. That is the claim, and it is now demonstrable in three commands.
The drift shape is a straight adjacent swap, like pricing's — but the
consequence is the inverse. In pricing, computing tax early makes a number
wrong. Here, deduplicating after normalising makes the system *lose* an event
it should have kept, and the evidence of the loss is the thing that was
deleted. A wrong number is discovered. A missing row is not.
`receive` and `replay` are drawn as this role's boundary (see brief.data.json
`given`), so MENTOR reports `receive` as planned-but-never-built. That is
correct and incomplete on its own: only the checkpoint spec knows that box was
somebody else's, which is why MCP-1 sends `given` inside the spec.
derivedFrom: git log --follow build/ingest.js, first touch per component

steps.summary: Mapped the incoming event onto the table's columns and applied defaults.
steps.note: Plan puts normalise second, after deduplicate. Built first. This is the drift — from here on, every comparison downstream sees the reshaped event rather than the one the sender actually sent.

steps.summary: Checked for a previously seen event — but against the normalised form, because that was what existed by then.
Wrote one row per event that survived the dedupe check.
Ran the acceptance tests: the duplicate case and the defaults case pass, the distinct-ids case does not.

failure.test: a2 — two different events, identical payloads, different ids
failure.message: dropped a distinct event as a duplicate: expected 2 rows, got 1
failure.whyItHidUntilNow: a1 sends the same event twice, which collapses to one row whichever order you deduplicate in. a3 sends a single event, so there is nothing to compare it against. a2 is the only criterion where 'the same event' computed before normalisation and after it give different answers — and normalisation is what drops the sender's id.
